title: Resting Tachycardia Detection
interpretation: Heart rate above 100 bpm while sedentary and at rest may indicate tachycardia. In the absence of stimulants, fever, or anxiety, sustained resting HR above 100 warrants medical review. Context matters: recent caffeine, dehydration, or medication changes can cause transient elevations.
recommended_agent_action: Flag as concern if sustained for 10+ minutes at rest. Ask user about caffeine, hydration, and recent medication changes.
what_not_to_conclude: Do not diagnose tachycardia or arrhythmia. A single elevated reading is not diagnostic.
sources: AHA Guidelines on Heart Rate Monitoring
Mayo Clinic - Tachycardia Overview

title: Exercise Heart Rate Response
interpretation: Heart rate naturally increases during physical activity. Expected range depends on age and fitness level. Maximum HR is commonly estimated as 220 minus age. Failure to reach expected HR during exercise or excessively rapid HR response may indicate deconditioning or cardiovascular concern.
recommended_agent_action: Log as normal if HR is within expected exercise range. Only flag if HR exceeds age-predicted maximum or fails to recover within 2 minutes post-exercise.
what_not_to_conclude: Do not conclude cardiac pathology from exercise-induced HR alone without recovery data.
sources: ACSM Exercise Guidelines
CDC Physical Activity Guidelines

title: Nocturnal Heart Rate Elevation
interpretation: Heart rate during sleep is typically 10-20% lower than daytime resting HR. Nocturnal HR elevation above daytime resting baseline while sleeping may indicate autonomic dysfunction, sleep apnea, illness onset, or stress response. Combined with low HRV, this pattern is more significant.
recommended_agent_action: Compare with user's typical sleeping HR. If 20%+ above sleeping baseline for multiple nights, escalate concern. Cross-reference with sleep quality and breathing rate.
what_not_to_conclude: Do not diagnose sleep disorders or cardiac conditions from nocturnal HR alone.
sources: Sleep Medicine Reviews - Nocturnal HR Patterns
European Heart Journal - HRV During Sleep

title: HRV Declining Trend
interpretation: A sustained decline in HRV over 7 or more days suggests increasing sympathetic nervous system dominance. This correlates with accumulated stress, inadequate recovery, illness onset, or overtraining. HRV is one of the most sensitive early indicators of physiological stress load.
recommended_agent_action: Track HRV trend over 7+ days. If decline exceeds 25% from personal baseline, notify user with context about recovery and stress management. Do not alarm.
what_not_to_conclude: Do not conclude specific disease from HRV decline. HRV varies significantly between individuals and with age.
sources: Task Force of ESC/NASPE - HRV Standards
Frontiers in Physiology - HRV and Stress

title: Acute Nocturnal HR Spike While Sedentary
interpretation: A sudden HR increase of 50%+ above resting baseline while sedentary at night, combined with HRV drop of 50%+, is a high-severity pattern. In elderly users, this combination at night with no corresponding movement can indicate acute cardiac event, panic attack, or severe pain episode.
recommended_agent_action: Immediate Level 5 alert. Notify emergency contact. Cross-reference SpO2, breathing rate, and EDA. If SpO2 also dropping, this is critical.
what_not_to_conclude: Do not diagnose heart attack or stroke. The agent identifies the pattern; medical professionals diagnose.
sources: AHA Emergency Cardiac Care Guidelines
Lancet - Wearable Detection of Cardiac Events

title: Heart Rate Recovery Assessment
interpretation: Heart rate recovery (HRR) is measured as the drop in HR from peak exercise to 1 minute post-exercise. An HRR of less than 12 bpm in the first minute is considered abnormal and is associated with increased cardiovascular mortality risk. Normal HRR is 15-25 bpm drop in the first minute.
recommended_agent_action: Track HRR after exercise sessions. If consistently below 12 bpm recovery in first minute, flag as pattern and suggest user discuss with healthcare provider.
what_not_to_conclude: Do not diagnose cardiac disease from HRR alone. Fitness level, medication, and environmental conditions affect HRR.
sources: NEJM - Heart Rate Recovery and Mortality
Journal of Cardiology - HRR Prognostic Value

title: Chronic Low HRV with Elevated Stress
interpretation: Persistently low HRV combined with elevated stress scores over multiple days reflects chronic sympathetic activation. This pattern is commonly seen in burnout, chronic stress, anxiety disorders, and early stages of illness. The body is in a sustained fight-or-flight state with insufficient parasympathetic recovery.
recommended_agent_action: If HRV below personal baseline by 30%+ and stress above baseline by 40%+ for 5+ consecutive days, escalate to Level 3. Suggest recovery activities and ask about recent life stressors.
what_not_to_conclude: Do not diagnose anxiety disorder or burnout syndrome. These are clinical diagnoses requiring professional evaluation.
sources: Psychosomatic Medicine - HRV and Chronic Stress
WHO - Burnout Definition ICD-11

title: Morning Resting HR as Health Indicator
interpretation: Morning resting heart rate measured within 5 minutes of waking is the most reliable HR baseline. An upward trend over multiple days may indicate accumulated fatigue, illness onset, or overtraining. A downward trend over weeks typically indicates improving cardiovascular fitness.
recommended_agent_action: Use morning HR as primary baseline. Track 7-day moving average. Alert if morning HR rises 10%+ above 14-day average for 3+ consecutive days.
what_not_to_conclude: Do not attribute morning HR changes to a single cause. Multiple factors including sleep quality, hydration, and alcohol affect morning HR.
sources: European Journal of Applied Physiology - Morning HR
Sports Medicine - Resting HR Monitoring

title: Bradycardia Detection
interpretation: Resting heart rate consistently below 50 bpm in non-athletes may indicate bradycardia. In trained athletes, resting HR of 40-50 bpm is normal due to increased cardiac efficiency. Context of fitness level and medication use (beta-blockers) is essential for interpretation.
recommended_agent_action: Check user profile for athletic status and medications. If non-athlete with sustained HR below 50, flag for medical review. If athlete, log as normal variant.
what_not_to_conclude: Do not diagnose bradycardia or heart block. Low HR in athletes is a normal physiological adaptation.
sources: AHA - Bradycardia Guidelines
British Journal of Sports Medicine - Athlete HR

title: HRV-Recovery Score Divergence
interpretation: When HRV drops significantly but recovery score remains stable (or vice versa), it may indicate that one metric is being influenced by factors not captured by the other. For example, good sleep may maintain recovery score while psychological stress suppresses HRV. This divergence warrants closer monitoring.
recommended_agent_action: Track both HRV and recovery score trends. If they diverge by more than 2 standard deviations for 3+ days, flag as an insight and ask user about non-physical stressors.
what_not_to_conclude: Do not assume recovery score alone reflects full physiological recovery. HRV captures autonomic balance that recovery algorithms may miss.
sources: Applied Psychophysiology and Biofeedback - HRV Measures
Journal of Sports Sciences - Recovery Monitoring
